# Forensic Dossier — OPmobility SE (OPM.PA)

*A deep dive on management and the setup. Source: the 2025 annual-results call (held 2026-02-25, first call with new CEO Félicie Burelle), cross-referenced against the screener's hard financials. Only one full transcript was available, so the multi-quarter "arc" is read against the multi-year financial trajectory rather than across several calls.*

OPmobility is the company formerly known as Plastic Omnium — a French Tier-1 auto-parts supplier (a Tier-1 sells finished systems straight to carmakers). It makes car exteriors and lighting (bumpers, body panels, headlamps), structural "modules" (assembled front-ends and electrification modules), and clean-energy "Powertrain" parts (fuel tanks plus hydrogen storage). Roughly €11.5 billion of economic revenue in 2025, half of it in Europe.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells is one of disciplined, family-stewarded resilience in a brutal end-market. The new CEO opened her first call by leaning hard on heritage — "very strong family and engaged values, long-term commitment, financial discipline" — and framed 2025 as proof that the strategy works through the cycle. The throughline is diversification away from a shrinking European base: two-thirds of 2025 order intake targeted regions outside Europe, with management repeatedly pointing to North America (28% of sales) and Asia (~20%) as the growth engines while Europe (half of revenue) is something to "consolidate," not grow.

Three growth drivers are introduced and pushed: (1) clean-energy Powertrain — fuel-tank share climbing "from 21% to 23%" with a "30% by 2030" target, plus hydrogen for heavy mobility; (2) modules, called "the fastest-growing segment" at ~6% growth, led by Korea; and (3) a new, still-vague "beyond automotive" leg (battery packs, hydrogen, and an intriguing single robotaxi customer). The load-bearing corporate-action item is a just-announced exploration to buy Hyundai Mobis's lighting business — management's bet to fix a lighting unit that has been a persistent drag.

What is quietly de-emphasized: the European core, the lighting unit's recent history, and the hydrogen timeline. Management never volunteers that lighting and hydrogen are loss-making sub-divisions; that only surfaced later, from the rating agency.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (2025 call) | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Very solid… significantly improving versus 2024," EBITDA over €1B "first time since 2019" | Net income €185M, up ~9% from €170M; revenue €10.22-11.5B, roughly flat (-2.6% YoY on the screener's basis); 5-yr EPS growth ~10.6% CAGR | Broadly fair on profit direction, but the "very solid" framing oversells a business that is barely growing revenue and runs a 1.8% net margin and ~9.4% gross margin |
| Free cash flow "almost reaching €300M… up an impressive 20%" | Annual FCF €297M; screener FCF margin 4.4%; trailing-twelve-month free cash flow €921M (a figure inflated by working-capital timing, not run-rate earnings power) | The €297M is real and improved; the €921M trailing figure should be treated with caution, not as steady-state |
| "In line with deleveraging… debt reduced by €167M to €1.4B"; net-debt-to-EBITDA 1.7x → 1.4x | Net debt recomputed at €1.4-1.51B (total debt €2.25B minus €730M cash) — a genuine liability | Verified, with corrections: deleveraging is real but the balance sheet is still levered, and S&P put the rating outlook on negative two months later |
| Returns/quality strong; "robust financial structure" | Return on equity 8.1%, return on invested capital (ROIC) 6.0% — below the ~8-10% cost of capital; Piotroski 8/9 (good accounting quality), Altman-Z 3.2 (solvent) | The accounting quality is genuinely good, but ROIC below cost of capital means the business, as a whole, does not earn its keep — a core value-trap tell |
| Beat-rate / guidance delivery | Screener shows beat 0 of 7 quarters (0%) | A real red flag the call never addresses — management hits annual targets it sets low, but does not beat the street quarter to quarter |

The single most important divergence: management's confident "resilience" framing sits on top of a business earning a ~6% ROIC against a ~9% cost of capital, with two named sub-divisions (lighting, hydrogen) losing money. The story is richer than the numbers justify.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Trajectory: **Stable-to-rising in tone, defensive in substance.** With only one call, the read is within-call rather than across quarters. The CEO's language is confident and offensive on the surface — "solid," "impressive," "flawless launches, 144 launches" — but the operational vocabulary is defensive: "cost reduction to sustain this pace," "decrease on our breakeven point," "mitigate the impact," "absorb all of the impact on foreign exchange." That is the language of a company defending margin in a falling-volume market, not one compounding. The most telling tonal tic is hedging on the dividend: asked directly whether the €0.49 payout would be defended in 2026, the CEO would not commit — "we always have a policy of serving dividend… that should remain the case" — which is a soft answer from a board that just cut the dividend from a high base.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium.** On the annual scorecard management is credible: it "took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did," and the 2025 numbers (EBITDA, FCF, deleveraging) match the targets reiterated through the year. That is real follow-through. But two things temper it: the 0-of-7 quarterly beat-rate (they guide to what they can hit, not above it — a sandbagging-to-meet pattern, not over-delivery), and the fact that the negative items (lighting/hydrogen losses, the rating-outlook risk) were left for outsiders to surface. Credibility on hitting a conservative number: high. Credibility on a clean, fully-disclosed picture: medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pressed exactly where the bodies are buried. Citi's Ross MacDonald pushed on (a) the 2026 free-cash-flow bridge and working-capital — management leaned on "WCR improvement, notably inventory management and payment terms," i.e. balance-sheet levers, not earnings; (b) the slow pace of fuel-tank share gains (21%→23% against a 30%-by-2030 target — implying the gains are back-end-loaded, a multi-year "trust us"); (c) the lighting acquisition's execution risk, explicitly recalling the painful Varroc lighting deal — management insisted "the situation is totally… not comparable." JPMorgan pressed on lighting growth and Stellantis volumes. The recurring deflection: the dividend question (non-committal) and the refusal to quantify the Hyundai Mobis balance-sheet impact. The topic analysts worry about that management under-addresses: whether the lighting unit can be fixed at all, and what a second large lighting deal does to an already-levered, negative-outlook balance sheet.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 ROIC ~6% below cost of capital — the whole company does not earn its cost of capital; cheapness risks being a value trap, not a bargain.
🔴 Two named loss-making sub-divisions (lighting and hydrogen) — confirmed by S&P, never volunteered on the call.
🔴 0-of-7 quarterly earnings beats — guides to hit, never to beat.
🔴 Dividend just cut to €0.49 and not firmly defended for 2026; €0.49 was already paid (ex-date 28 April, paid 30 April 2026) — the distribution is behind us, not ahead.
🔴 S&P revised the rating outlook to negative (BB+) in 2026, citing lighting/hydrogen losses and the risk that cost cuts don't lift cash-flow-to-debt enough.
🔴 A second large lighting acquisition (Hyundai Mobis) layered onto a levered, negative-outlook balance sheet, after a prior lighting deal (Varroc) went badly.
🟢 Genuine deleveraging: net debt down €167M, leverage 1.7x → 1.4x.
🟢 Real geographic diversification working — North America +4.9% and Asia +7.3% in Q1 2026 offset European weakness; two-thirds of order intake now outside Europe.
🟢 Piotroski 8/9 and Altman-Z 3.2 — clean accounting and solvent.
🟢 Modules genuinely growing ~6%; fuel-tank share genuinely climbing.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The terminology is migrating from "automotive supplier" toward "mobility / beyond automotive," which is both an honest acknowledgment that core light-vehicle volume is structurally soft and a hint that management knows the ICE-linked base (fuel tanks, plastic body parts) faces a long secular fade. The single robotaxi customer name-drop ("1 player with whom we are today engaged… the business model there will be pretty different") is an option, not a number. The capital-allocation signal worth weighing: with the balance sheet already levered and the rating on negative outlook, management is choosing to spend on another lighting acquisition rather than aggressively pay down debt or defend the dividend — a growth-over-balance-sheet tilt that the rating agency is explicitly nervous about.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a competent, family-controlled cyclical defending margins and deleveraging in a falling-volume market — neither strengthening into a compounder nor deteriorating into distress.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this business earns a ~6% return on invested capital against a ~9% cost of capital, with two loss-making sub-divisions and a negative rating outlook — so the ~4x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple is cheap *because the underlying base is structurally low-return and ICE-linked*, not because the market is missing hidden earnings power. The load-bearing "catalyst," the Hyundai Mobis lighting acquisition, is at the non-binding exploration stage and, if it closes, adds integration risk to a levered balance sheet rather than crystallizing value.

Moat: **NARROW**, and on balance **ERODING**. The moat is real but thin — switching-costs from being designed-in to multi-year vehicle platforms and scale in plastic exteriors — but the evidence (ROIC below cost of capital, ~9.4% gross margin, 1.8% net margin) is the signature of a low-return commodity-parts business, and the returns are not rising. Secular threat: **material** (not yet terminal) — the energy transition slowly erodes the ICE-linked fuel-tank and plastic-component base, even as hydrogen and modules offer a partial, unproven offset.

*A deep dive on management and the setup. Source: the 2025 annual-results call (held 2026-02-25, first call with new CEO Félicie Burelle), cross-referenced against the screener's hard financials. Only one full transcript was available, so the multi-quarter "arc" is read against the multi-year financial trajectory rather than across several calls.*

OPmobility is the company formerly known as Plastic Omnium — a French Tier-1 auto-parts supplier (a Tier-1 sells finished systems straight to carmakers). It makes car exteriors and lighting (bumpers, body panels, headlamps), structural "modules" (assembled front-ends and electrification modules), and clean-energy "Powertrain" parts (fuel tanks plus hydrogen storage). Roughly €11.5 billion of economic revenue in 2025, half of it in Europe.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells is one of disciplined, family-stewarded resilience in a brutal end-market. The new CEO opened her first call by leaning hard on heritage — "very strong family and engaged values, long-term commitment, financial discipline" — and framed 2025 as proof that the strategy works through the cycle. The throughline is diversification away from a shrinking European base: two-thirds of 2025 order intake targeted regions outside Europe, with management repeatedly pointing to North America (28% of sales) and Asia (~20%) as the growth engines while Europe (half of revenue) is something to "consolidate," not grow.

Three growth drivers are introduced and pushed: (1) clean-energy Powertrain — fuel-tank share climbing "from 21% to 23%" with a "30% by 2030" target, plus hydrogen for heavy mobility; (2) modules, called "the fastest-growing segment" at ~6% growth, led by Korea; and (3) a new, still-vague "beyond automotive" leg (battery packs, hydrogen, and an intriguing single robotaxi customer). The load-bearing corporate-action item is a just-announced exploration to buy Hyundai Mobis's lighting business — management's bet to fix a lighting unit that has been a persistent drag.

What is quietly de-emphasized: the European core, the lighting unit's recent history, and the hydrogen timeline. Management never volunteers that lighting and hydrogen are loss-making sub-divisions; that only surfaced later, from the rating agency.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (2025 call) | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Very solid… significantly improving versus 2024," EBITDA over €1B "first time since 2019" | Net income €185M, up ~9% from €170M; revenue €10.22-11.5B, roughly flat (-2.6% YoY on the screener's basis); 5-yr EPS growth ~10.6% CAGR | Broadly fair on profit direction, but the "very solid" framing oversells a business that is barely growing revenue and runs a 1.8% net margin and ~9.4% gross margin |
| Free cash flow "almost reaching €300M… up an impressive 20%" | Annual FCF €297M; screener FCF margin 4.4%; trailing-twelve-month free cash flow €921M (a figure inflated by working-capital timing, not run-rate earnings power) | The €297M is real and improved; the €921M trailing figure should be treated with caution, not as steady-state |
| "In line with deleveraging… debt reduced by €167M to €1.4B"; net-debt-to-EBITDA 1.7x → 1.4x | Net debt recomputed at €1.4-1.51B (total debt €2.25B minus €730M cash) — a genuine liability | Verified, with corrections: deleveraging is real but the balance sheet is still levered, and S&P put the rating outlook on negative two months later |
| Returns/quality strong; "robust financial structure" | Return on equity 8.1%, return on invested capital (ROIC) 6.0% — below the ~8-10% cost of capital; Piotroski 8/9 (good accounting quality), Altman-Z 3.2 (solvent) | The accounting quality is genuinely good, but ROIC below cost of capital means the business, as a whole, does not earn its keep — a core value-trap tell |
| Beat-rate / guidance delivery | Screener shows beat 0 of 7 quarters (0%) | A real red flag the call never addresses — management hits annual targets it sets low, but does not beat the street quarter to quarter |

The single most important divergence: management's confident "resilience" framing sits on top of a business earning a ~6% ROIC against a ~9% cost of capital, with two named sub-divisions (lighting, hydrogen) losing money. The story is richer than the numbers justify.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Trajectory: **Stable-to-rising in tone, defensive in substance.** With only one call, the read is within-call rather than across quarters. The CEO's language is confident and offensive on the surface — "solid," "impressive," "flawless launches, 144 launches" — but the operational vocabulary is defensive: "cost reduction to sustain this pace," "decrease on our breakeven point," "mitigate the impact," "absorb all of the impact on foreign exchange." That is the language of a company defending margin in a falling-volume market, not one compounding. The most telling tonal tic is hedging on the dividend: asked directly whether the €0.49 payout would be defended in 2026, the CEO would not commit — "we always have a policy of serving dividend… that should remain the case" — which is a soft answer from a board that just cut the dividend from a high base.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium.** On the annual scorecard management is credible: it "took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did," and the 2025 numbers (EBITDA, FCF, deleveraging) match the targets reiterated through the year. That is real follow-through. But two things temper it: the 0-of-7 quarterly beat-rate (they guide to what they can hit, not above it — a sandbagging-to-meet pattern, not over-delivery), and the fact that the negative items (lighting/hydrogen losses, the rating-outlook risk) were left for outsiders to surface. Credibility on hitting a conservative number: high. Credibility on a clean, fully-disclosed picture: medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pressed exactly where the bodies are buried. Citi's Ross MacDonald pushed on (a) the 2026 free-cash-flow bridge and working-capital — management leaned on "WCR improvement, notably inventory management and payment terms," i.e. balance-sheet levers, not earnings; (b) the slow pace of fuel-tank share gains (21%→23% against a 30%-by-2030 target — implying the gains are back-end-loaded, a multi-year "trust us"); (c) the lighting acquisition's execution risk, explicitly recalling the painful Varroc lighting deal — management insisted "the situation is totally… not comparable." JPMorgan pressed on lighting growth and Stellantis volumes. The recurring deflection: the dividend question (non-committal) and the refusal to quantify the Hyundai Mobis balance-sheet impact. The topic analysts worry about that management under-addresses: whether the lighting unit can be fixed at all, and what a second large lighting deal does to an already-levered, negative-outlook balance sheet.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 ROIC ~6% below cost of capital — the whole company does not earn its cost of capital; cheapness risks being a value trap, not a bargain.
🔴 Two named loss-making sub-divisions (lighting and hydrogen) — confirmed by S&P, never volunteered on the call.
🔴 0-of-7 quarterly earnings beats — guides to hit, never to beat.
🔴 Dividend just cut to €0.49 and not firmly defended for 2026; €0.49 was already paid (ex-date 28 April, paid 30 April 2026) — the distribution is behind us, not ahead.
🔴 S&P revised the rating outlook to negative (BB+) in 2026, citing lighting/hydrogen losses and the risk that cost cuts don't lift cash-flow-to-debt enough.
🔴 A second large lighting acquisition (Hyundai Mobis) layered onto a levered, negative-outlook balance sheet, after a prior lighting deal (Varroc) went badly.
🟢 Genuine deleveraging: net debt down €167M, leverage 1.7x → 1.4x.
🟢 Real geographic diversification working — North America +4.9% and Asia +7.3% in Q1 2026 offset European weakness; two-thirds of order intake now outside Europe.
🟢 Piotroski 8/9 and Altman-Z 3.2 — clean accounting and solvent.
🟢 Modules genuinely growing ~6%; fuel-tank share genuinely climbing.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The terminology is migrating from "automotive supplier" toward "mobility / beyond automotive," which is both an honest acknowledgment that core light-vehicle volume is structurally soft and a hint that management knows the ICE-linked base (fuel tanks, plastic body parts) faces a long secular fade. The single robotaxi customer name-drop ("1 player with whom we are today engaged… the business model there will be pretty different") is an option, not a number. The capital-allocation signal worth weighing: with the balance sheet already levered and the rating on negative outlook, management is choosing to spend on another lighting acquisition rather than aggressively pay down debt or defend the dividend — a growth-over-balance-sheet tilt that the rating agency is explicitly nervous about.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a competent, family-controlled cyclical defending margins and deleveraging in a falling-volume market — neither strengthening into a compounder nor deteriorating into distress.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this business earns a ~6% return on invested capital against a ~9% cost of capital, with two loss-making sub-divisions and a negative rating outlook — so the ~4x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple is cheap *because the underlying base is structurally low-return and ICE-linked*, not because the market is missing hidden earnings power. The load-bearing "catalyst," the Hyundai Mobis lighting acquisition, is at the non-binding exploration stage and, if it closes, adds integration risk to a levered balance sheet rather than crystallizing value.

Moat: **NARROW**, and on balance **ERODING**. The moat is real but thin — switching-costs from being designed-in to multi-year vehicle platforms and scale in plastic exteriors — but the evidence (ROIC below cost of capital, ~9.4% gross margin, 1.8% net margin) is the signature of a low-return commodity-parts business, and the returns are not rising. Secular threat: **material** (not yet terminal) — the energy transition slowly erodes the ICE-linked fuel-tank and plastic-component base, even as hydrogen and modules offer a partial, unproven offset.

bull_thesis: OPmobility is a competent, family-controlled French auto-parts supplier (the former Plastic Omnium) trading at roughly four times free cash flow, a depressed multiple that prices in terminal decline for a business that is actually deleveraging and quietly diversifying. The strongest evidence: 2025 was a genuine improvement year, with net income up about 9% to 185 million euros, free cash flow up about 20% to 297 million euros, and core operating profit (EBITDA) crossing 1 billion euros for the first time since 2019, all hit in line with the targets management set and reiterated through the year. Net debt fell by 167 million euros and leverage dropped from 1.7 to 1.4 times. Underneath the soft European core, the growth legs are real and verifiable in the most recent quarter: North American sales rose about 5% and Asian sales about 7% in the first quarter of 2026, offsetting Europe, and two-thirds of new order intake now targets regions outside Europe. The modules segment is growing roughly 6%, and fuel-tank (clean-energy Powertrain) market share is climbing toward a 30%-by-2030 target. The accounting is clean (Piotroski 8 of 9) and the company is solvent (Altman-Z 3.2). On the parts, even a conservative distressed-peer multiple on the four segments, less the net debt, lands at or above the current price, so the downside to a defensible floor is modest while a cyclical recovery in European light-vehicle volumes plus a successful fix of the lighting unit would re-rate the equity meaningfully. The case requires three things to hold: European volumes stabilize rather than keep falling, the lighting and hydrogen sub-divisions stop bleeding cash, and the balance sheet does not deteriorate further.
bear_thesis: The four-times-free-cash-flow multiple is cheap because the business does not earn its keep, and the discount is shared sector beta, not hidden value. Return on invested capital is about 6% against a roughly 9% cost of capital, gross margin is a razor-thin 9.4%, and net margin is 1.8% — the textbook signature of a low-return, commoditized parts business, not a temporarily mispriced compounder. Two named sub-divisions, lighting and hydrogen, are losing money, a fact management never volunteered on the call and which only surfaced when S&P revised the credit-rating outlook to negative (affirming BB+) in 2026, citing exactly those losses and the risk that cost cuts will not lift cash-flow-to-debt enough. The company has beaten quarterly estimates zero times in the last seven quarters — it guides to numbers it can hit, never above them. The dividend was already cut to 0.49 euros, paid out at the end of April 2026, and management would not firmly commit to defending it for 2026. The load-bearing corporate-action item, the proposed purchase of Hyundai Mobis's lighting business, is only a non-binding exploration (a memorandum of understanding signed in late January 2026, OPmobility named preferred bidder at an estimated 350 million dollars), and if it closes it layers integration risk onto an already-levered, negative-outlook balance sheet — echoing the painful Varroc lighting deal management was forced to defend on the call. The deepest risk is structural: the ICE-linked fuel-tank and plastic-body-part base faces a slow secular fade as the vehicle fleet electrifies, so a low multiple on a slowly shrinking, sub-cost-of-capital base is a value trap, not a bargain. The stock fell about 17% in June 2026 on European auto-sector pressure — confirming there is no idiosyncratic floor here, only sector gravity.
consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the right question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into stable earnings power. Here it is not mispriced — the market is roughly right. The street's price target spread (low 10, high 21, average ~17.4 euros) brackets the stock, and the consensus forward EPS-growth figure of about +15% is plausibly optimistic given a 0-of-7 quarterly beat record and a business whose return on invested capital (about 6%) sits below its cost of capital (about 9%). The one genuine disagreement worth naming is that some bulls treat the trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of 921 million euros as run-rate earnings power; that figure is inflated by working-capital timing and is not steady-state — the durable free cash flow is the ~297 million euros annual figure, and management itself flagged that 2026 free cash flow leans on working-capital levers (inventory, payment terms), not earnings. There is no hidden upside the market is missing; if anything the market may still be under-pricing the structural ICE fade and the lighting/hydrogen losses.
forcing_function: There is no hard, dated event that forces a re-rating. The nearest candidate, the Hyundai Mobis lighting acquisition, is only a non-binding exploration: a memorandum of understanding signed in late January 2026 with OPmobility named preferred bidder at an estimated 350 million dollars, targeting a definitive agreement sometime in 2026 — a soft, serially-extendable, single-counterparty deal with no contractual payout and, even if signed, integration rather than crystallization. Next earnings is about three weeks out (first-half 2026 results), but that is a data point, not a catalyst, and the beat record is 0 of 7. The real re-rating would require a multi-year European volume recovery and a demonstrated lighting/hydrogen turnaround — neither of which is dated or binding.
valley_of_death: The next three-to-nine months carry real, dated downside before any re-rating. First, European light-vehicle production guidance was cut again and the stock already fell about 17% in June 2026 on sector pressure — the volume backdrop is deteriorating, not stabilizing. Second, S&P's negative outlook (affirmed BB+ in 2026) is a live downgrade clock: the agency wants cash-flow-to-debt well above 20% and free-cash-flow-to-debt near 10% in 2026, and a miss — easy if European volumes keep sliding and lighting/hydrogen keep losing money — triggers a downgrade that raises borrowing costs on a 2.25-billion-euro debt load. Third, the November 2026 dual macro hard-date in the current regime (China tariff-suspension expiry plus the U.S. Supreme Court tariff ruling) directly threatens an auto supplier with cross-border supply chains and Mexican/Chinese exposure. Fourth, the proposed Hyundai Mobis lighting acquisition, if it firms up, is a cash outflow and integration risk layered onto a levered, negative-outlook balance sheet. The dividend is already paid, so there is no near-term distribution to cushion the wait.
positioning_washout: Limited mechanical-selling dynamics to exploit. This is a family-controlled French mid-cap (the Burelle family), so the controlling block is sticky and not a forced seller. The dividend was already cut and paid, so the yield-focused shareholder exodus that can force liquidation has largely happened rather than lying ahead. A credit-rating downgrade from S&P could force some rating-sensitive bond and crossover holders to trim, and continued European-auto-sector outflows would pressure the equity passively, but there is no single dated forced-selling event (no index deletion, no covenant trip, no lock-up expiry) that creates a clean wash-out entry. The June 2026 drop was sector beta, not a one-name capitulation.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. OPmobility is a well-run, clean-accounting, deleveraging cyclical, but at 13.64 euros it trades at roughly its base-case sum-of-the-parts fair value of about 11 euros — a small premium, not a discount, once the ~1.5-billion-euro net debt is correctly subtracted instead of mistaken for net cash. The optical 4x price-to-free-cash-flow is cheap because the whole business earns about 6% on invested capital against a ~9% cost of capital, with two loss-making sub-divisions and an ICE-linked base facing a slow secular fade — the cheapness is shared European-auto-parts sector beta, not idiosyncratic edge, and Forvia screens cheaper still. The load-bearing catalyst is a soft, non-binding lighting acquisition that, if it closes, adds risk rather than crystallizing value. Against the current regime — which rewards hard-dated, structurally-independent special situations (forced-sellers, spinoffs, distressed) and explicitly penalizes theses that hinge on a cyclical recovery or one shared macro factor — this name is the wrong shape: its upside depends on a European-volume rebound and a lighting fix, both undated, while the November 2026 tariff/Supreme-Court dual hard-date and a live S&P downgrade clock threaten the downside first. Risk/reward is unfavorable (about -53% to the adverse case, +21% to the favorable, base case below today's price). Pass on the catalyst-overlay view; the underlying value case is merely fair-to-slightly-cheap, capped by an eroding narrow moat and a material energy-transition threat — not a value buy, a value hold at best, and only on a meaningful pullback.
sop_breakdown: Base-case sum-of-the-parts at roughly 11 euros per share, blending the favorable (~16.5) and adverse (~6.4) scenarios toward the middle and anchoring on the independent intrinsic models that cluster there (Buffett/owner-earnings fair value ~11.4, the screener's fair value ~11.4). Enterprise value of about 3.0 billion euros: Exterior & Lighting ~1.2B (0.23x sales, lighting still a drag), Modules ~1.05B (0.29x, the one genuine grower), Powertrain/clean-energy ~0.75B (0.29x, share gains offset by hydrogen losses and the ICE fade). Less the ~1.5B net-debt liability = ~1.5-1.6B equity, about 11 euros per share — essentially the current price of 13.64, i.e. the stock is close to fair, with a slight premium, not a discount, once the debt is properly subtracted rather than added back.
risk_reward: Roughly symmetric-to-unfavorable. Downside to the adverse parts value is about -53% (13.64 to ~6.4); upside to the favorable parts value is about +21% (13.64 to ~16.5); base-case fair value of ~11 sits about 19% BELOW the current price. So at today's price the buyer is paying a small premium to base-case intrinsic value for an option on European volume recovery and a lighting fix — a poor risk/reward, with more room to fall than to rise.
peer_comps_note: The peer set is the depressed European and global Tier-1 auto-parts cohort — Forvia (FRVIA.PA), Faurecia legacy (FR.PA), Lear, Aptiv, Autoliv, Magna, BorgWarner. OPmobility at ~4x price-to-free-cash-flow is broadly in line to slightly cheap versus this cohort, but Forvia screens materially cheaper still (sub-1x P/FCF, ~78% discount to intrinsic) and Faurecia is outright distressed. Critically, this is a sector-wide regulatory-and-structural de-rate: the whole European auto-parts complex is repricing together on the ICE-to-EV transition, OEM volume cuts, and tariff uncertainty, so the gap to peers is shared sector beta (a common-factor move), NOT name-specific edge. The June 2026 ~17% drop hit the whole group; OPmobility has no idiosyncratic discount to harvest here.

# Forensic Dossier — OPmobility SE (OPM.PA)

*A deep dive on management and the setup. Single transcript available: the 2025 full-year results call, 25 February 2026. Where only one call exists, the "trajectory across quarters" sections lean on the multi-year financial trajectory the screener supplies rather than on quarter-to-quarter tone shifts.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

OPmobility is the French auto-parts supplier formerly known as Plastic Omnium, rebranded in 2023. It makes car exteriors and lighting, plastic modules, and fuel/energy systems (its "C-Power" clean-energy business — fuel tanks today, battery packs and hydrogen storage tomorrow). The 2025 results call is the first led by new Chief Executive Félicie Burelle, a member of the founding family, and the story she tells is one of continuity and disciplined execution rather than reinvention: "we have been shaping our company over generation with very strong family and engaged values, long-term commitment, financial discipline."

The core message is resilience in a weak market. Global auto production was soft and the mix shifted hard by region ("Asia representing 50% of the market"), yet management delivered on every stated 2025 target: earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) crossed €1 billion "for the first time since 2019," operating margin rose to €490 million, net income reached €185 million, and free cash flow (the cash left after running and investing in the business) hit €297 million, up 20%. The through-line is deleveraging — net-debt-to-EBITDA fell from 1.7x to 1.4x — paired with a cautious pivot toward "future mobility": electrification, hydrogen, and even a nascent robotaxi supply relationship.

The single genuinely new strategic thread is the lighting business. Management is trying to fix an acquisition it clearly regrets — the 2022 Varroc lighting deal, described obliquely as having come with "the poor order book prior to the acquisition." The proposed remedy is a much larger tie-up with Hyundai Mobis' lighting arm (an MoU signed January 2026), which Burelle is at pains to distinguish from Varroc: "a very sizable business with one leading OEM... more than 90% of its sales engaged with that."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (2025 call) | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Very strong… significantly improving vs 2024" | Net income €170M→€185M (+9%); EPS €1.18→€1.30 (+10%); FCF +20% | **Supported** on profit and cash, but off a low base — net margin is only ~1.8% |
| Revenue resilience / "enjoyed some growth" | Reported revenue −2.6% year-on-year (€10.48B→€10.22B); +1.7% "like-for-like" after €300M of currency drag | **Mixed** — organic growth is real but low-single-digit; the headline is a decline |
| Deleveraging discipline | Net debt reduced €167M to ~€1.4-1.5B; net-debt/EBITDA 1.7x→1.4x | **Supported** — the balance sheet is genuinely improving |
| Free-cash-flow strength (€297M) | Trailing-twelve-month FCF €921M per the screener; price-to-FCF ~4x | **Supported and then some** — cash generation is the strongest part of the story |
| "Reached all of our targets" | Guidance was met; but the screener flags an earnings-beat rate of **0 of 7 quarters (0%)** against consensus | **Tension** — they hit their *own* guidance but have not beaten the *street* once |

The standout disconnect: management frames a −2.6% revenue year as a win. It is defensible (currency did most of the damage, and they grew organically), but a newcomer should read "very solid results" as "held the line and cut costs well," not "grew." Profitability improved because breakeven came down, not because the top line expanded. Return on invested capital (ROIC — the profit earned per dollar of capital put to work) is only ~6%, below a reasonable cost of capital — this business earns roughly what it costs to fund, which is the central fact of the whole case.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, from a defensive base.** With only one call, the read is on register rather than quarter-over-quarter drift. Burelle's language is confident but conspicuously defensive-flavored: the words that recur are "resilience," "flexibility," "cost reduction," "breakeven point," "grip on our cost." Chief Financial Officer Olivier Dabi leads with operational control — "a strong grip on our cost and a decrease on our breakeven point" — rather than demand or pricing power. That is the vocabulary of a company protecting margins in a shrinking market, not one riding a growth wave. The offensive notes (electrification, robotaxi, "beyond automotive") are framed as optionality for later, not current earnings drivers — "the beyond automotive only represents [a small share] of our sales."

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium.** The positive: management set 2025 KPI targets a year earlier, "reiterated [them] throughout the year," and delivered on all of them — EBITDA over €1B, FCF up double digits, leverage down. That is a clean year of doing what they said. The caveat the transcript cannot hide is the screener's beat rate of 0 of 7 quarters versus consensus: they meet their own bar but set it at or below where the street already is, so there is no upside-surprise culture here. For 2026 they guide to a stable ~35% tax rate and free-cash-flow growth funded by both operations and working-capital improvement ("inventory management and payment terms") — credible, incremental, unexciting.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three pressure points surface in the Q&A, and management's answers are telling:

- **Lighting execution risk.** Citi's Ross MacDonald directly invokes the Varroc scar: "given that the last acquisition in lighting, obviously, you had some execution headaches around the order bank." Burelle's rebuttal — the Hyundai Mobis business is "not comparable," a healthy captive vs. a "depressed business" — is plausible but unprovable until terms and the order book are disclosed. This is the key open risk.
- **The dividend.** MacDonald presses twice on whether the €0.49 dividend can be defended given the M&A cash call. Burelle never commits to the number, retreating to "we always have a policy of serving dividend to the shareholders. So that should remain the case." That is a non-answer on the *level* — a yield-focused holder should not assume €0.49 is safe if the Hyundai deal consumes cash.
- **Free-cash-flow quality.** MacDonald notes peers got a 2025 working-capital tailwind that OPmobility did not; management concedes and pledges a "dedicated initiative" on payment terms for 2026 — i.e., some of next year's FCF is engineered from the balance sheet, not pure operations.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Revenue is shrinking in reported terms (−2.6%) and margins are razor-thin (net ~1.8%); the business earns roughly its cost of capital (ROIC ~6%).
🔴 The 0-for-7 beat rate signals no positive-surprise dynamic — the market has no reason to be repeatedly surprised upward.
🔴 A second large lighting acquisition is being layered on right after the first (Varroc) went badly; terms and balance-sheet impact undisclosed, and it competes with the dividend for cash.
🔴 Deep cyclical and secular exposure: fuel tanks (C-Power) are an internal-combustion-linked product line whose terminal demand shrinks as vehicles electrify — management's own pivot to battery packs and hydrogen is an admission of this.

🟢 Genuine, sustained deleveraging (1.7x→1.4x) and record EBITDA/FCF — the balance sheet and cash engine are strengthening.
🟢 Piotroski score 8/9 and Altman-Z of 3.2 (a solvency measure — 3.2 is comfortably in the safe zone): the accounting quality and bankruptcy-distance are sound.
🟢 New-family CEO with a clear, disciplined operating playbook and a credible one-year delivery record.
🟢 Order intake diversifying — "2/3 of our order intake for 2025 is targeting regions outside Europe," and share gains in C-Power fuel tanks (21%→23%, targeting 30% by 2030).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most revealing shift is linguistic: the C-Power segment is now discussed as *consolidating a declining market* — "we consolidate in a market where players... are decreasing, even disappearing." That is gaining share of a shrinking pie, which is a value-trap tell for the fuel-systems business even as it flatters near-term share statistics. Second, the robotaxi comment — "the business model there will be pretty different from our conventional market" — is management quietly acknowledging that its highest-growth future opportunity carries economics it does not yet understand. Third, the dividend deflection combined with the M&A push signals that capital allocation priorities are shifting from shareholder returns toward reinvestment/consolidation — a rational choice for a sub-cost-of-capital business, but one that the current yield-oriented holder base may not welcome.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE**, tilting toward a disciplined deleveraging story with a low-return core. Management is executing well on the things it controls — cost, cash, leverage — but the underlying business is a low-margin, low-return, cyclically- and secularly-pressured auto supplier growing at low-single digits at best. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a "cheap because the returns are structurally mediocre" situation, not a "cheap because misunderstood" one.** The ~4x price-to-free-cash-flow and multi-method margin-of-safety look seductive, but ROIC ~6% means the market is correctly pricing a business that does not create much economic value per euro invested. The Hyundai Mobis lighting deal is the swing factor — done well it adds scale to a fixable segment; done like Varroc it destroys the deleveraging thesis and pressures the dividend.

**Economic moat: NARROW, trending toward ERODING.** The moat type is scale-cost and switching-cost (deep, sticky OEM program engagement, 150 plants, multi-year platform awards). But the returns evidence undercuts any "wide" read: ROIC ~6% and net margin ~1.8% are the signature of a supplier with limited pricing power, squeezed between consolidating automakers above and raw-material/labor costs below. Gross margin is stable at ~9.4% but structurally thin. **Secular threat: material** (not yet terminal). The energy-transition force is real and specific here — the C-Power fuel-tank franchise (~a third of profit-relevant activity) is tied to internal-combustion vehicles, a demand pool that peaks and declines over the horizon. It is *material* rather than *terminal* only because management is actively redeploying that competence into battery packs and hydrogen storage, and because exteriors/lighting/modules are powertrain-agnostic. But a real chunk of the earnings base is a melting ICE-linked asset, which is exactly why the low multiple is deserved rather than a gift.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that the market is charging a distressed price for a business that is not distressed. OPmobility - the French supplier formerly called Plastic Omnium - makes the plastic parts on the outside of cars, headlamps, pre-assembled front-end modules and fuel and energy-storage systems. At EUR 12.77 on Euronext Paris the entire equity costs about EUR 1.83 billion. Against that sits roughly EUR 300 million a year of free cash flow on the company's own definition (EUR 297m in 2025, guided higher for 2026), which is a free-cash-flow yield near 16%, and about EUR 1.40 of likely 2026 earnings per share, which is under 9 times. Those are the prices you pay for a business you expect to shrink.

The evidence says it is not shrinking. Net profit has risen five years running, from EUR 126m in 2021 to EUR 185m in 2025. EBITDA passed EUR 1 billion in 2025 for the first time since 2019. Free cash flow rose 21% to EUR 297m. In the first half of 2026, reported on 22 July, revenue grew 0.4% on a like-for-like basis (stripping out currency and acquisitions) while global vehicle production fell 1.0%, net profit rose 13% to EUR 102m, and the operating margin held at 4.8% of sales. Full-year guidance - higher operating profit, higher net profit, higher free cash flow, lower debt - was reaffirmed unchanged for the third time this year.

The engine of the thesis is deleveraging, not growth. Net debt has gone EUR 1,577m (end 2024) to EUR 1,409m (end 2025) to EUR 1,320m at 30 June 2026, and leverage from 1.7 times EBITDA to 1.4 times. Debt is about 42% of the enterprise value here, so with the enterprise value unchanged, repaying EUR 150-200m of debt a year moves 8-11% a year across to the shareholder. Add a 3.8% dividend (EUR 0.49 per share, paid 30 April 2026) and the shareholder is being paid to wait while the balance sheet does the work.

The operating case has three specific supports. First, the fuel-tank business is consolidating a market that rivals are leaving: share went from 21% to 23% in 2025 against a 30% target for 2030, and management said in February 2026 that some competitors are 'decreasing, even disappearing'. It is also the highest-margin segment (5.5%) and it is currently being helped, not hurt, by slower electrification - a hybrid still needs a tank. Second, the lighting business, which has been the drag since the 2022 Varroc purchase came with a weak order book, finally inflected: seven launches in the first half of 2026 with more to come, and management calls 2025 'a low point in terms of sales' for that unit. Third, the customer base is being rebuilt where the volume actually is - two-thirds of 2025 order intake was outside Europe, and the awards named in July were Chery, Kia, Ford, Maruti Suzuki and Indian and Korean programmes rather than the European incumbents.

There is unpriced optionality in the proposed purchase of Hyundai Mobis's lighting business, a unit with more than EUR 1 billion of annual revenue, on which OPmobility signed a memorandum of understanding on 27 January 2026 and was named preferred bidder. If it lands at a sensible price it doubles the scale of the weakest division and hands OPmobility a direct commercial route into Hyundai and Kia, the fastest-growing volume group outside China.

What has to hold for this to work: resin and energy costs need to be recovered through contract indexation and negotiation within two to three quarters rather than permanently absorbed; the second half of 2026 has to generate cash from operations rather than from the working-capital and factoring pull that carried the first half; the Hyundai Mobis deal has to be signed at a price that does not interrupt debt repayment; and European vehicle production has to stop getting worse, not necessarily get better.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that this is an ordinary, low-return, leveraged cyclical whose cheapness is not a mispricing but a fair price, and that the next two or three quarters are the wrong ones to own it.

Start with quality. OPmobility converts EUR 10.2 billion of revenue into EUR 185 million of net profit - a 1.8% net margin - and earns about 6% on capital employed and 8.1% on equity. That is a business earning roughly its cost of capital and no more. Neither of the two earnings calls in the file addresses this, and no analyst asked. Tangible book value is effectively zero: shareholders' equity of EUR 2,119m at end-2025 is entirely accounted for by EUR 1,292m of goodwill and EUR 799m of other intangibles. There is no asset floor beneath the equity, only the cash flow.

Then the leverage. Net debt of EUR 1.32 billion sits against an equity value of about EUR 1.83 billion. That is the reason the equity screens cheap on earnings and free cash flow while the enterprise is priced roughly in line with its peers. The arithmetic is symmetrical and unforgiving: a 20% fall in enterprise value costs the shareholder about 35%.

The live risk is raw materials, and it is deteriorating. This is a polymer converter; resin and energy are its swing costs and they track oil. On the 22 July call management confirmed the first-half hit landed mainly in the second quarter, refused to size it - 'we won't comment too much on the amount' - said resin had a brief window of relief and is 'moving up again', and warned that 'the more the conflict last and it impacts the cost of energy and resin, the more it will be difficult for the whole industry to sustain over the long run'. Brent crude has risen roughly a quarter since early July on the reinstated Hormuz blockade. First-half operating profit was already 3.6% lower in euros than a year earlier despite flat revenue; the second half faces a worse cost base with no contracted recovery mechanism disclosed.

The cash-flow shape for the second half is the most likely place for a guidance miss, and the chief financial officer said so himself: the first half took close to EUR 100m of working-capital benefit, the second half will see lower factoring and the reversal of a supplier-payment initiative, so the free-cash-flow target has to be met out of operating cash generation while investment rises. Free cash flow of EUR 167m in the first half against a full-year target above EUR 297m leaves no room for the working capital to bite harder than planned.

The acquisition is a real balance-sheet risk, not just optionality. OPmobility is negotiating for a business with over EUR 1 billion of revenue while its own market capitalisation is EUR 1.8 billion, the price is undisclosed, and the only reassurance is verbal - 'we are taking the objective of that acquisition not to impact our deleveraging strategy'. That is an intention, not a term sheet. The precedent is unhelpful: the 2022 Varroc lighting purchase arrived with an order book so weak it took three years to work off, and management's answer to that comparison in February 2026 was assertion rather than evidence.

Two further costs are acknowledged and unquantified. Customer restructuring across European carmakers is accelerating, and management said in July that a heavier wave would force more of their own, but 'today, it's not embedded in our figures'. And the European local-content framework the company is lobbying for is undated, with the chief executive herself warning it might arrive 'a bit too late'.

Finally, there is no structural path to a forced re-rating. Burelle SA held 60.63% of the shares and 74.56% of the votes at 31 December 2025. There is no activist route, no takeover route and no break-up route. The float is roughly 38% of a EUR 1.8 billion company - about EUR 0.7 billion - which is thin enough that the stock can drift regardless of the fundamentals. That is visible in the tape: the shares rose about 4% to EUR 13.44 on the 22 July results and gave the whole move back within two sessions, closing 24 July at EUR 12.73, within 1% of the 52-week low.

What would confirm the bear: a third-quarter revenue update in late October showing no margin recovery on resin, or an acquisition announced at a price that lifts net debt back above EUR 1.5 billion.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not with the published analyst targets - five of six covering analysts rate the shares a buy and the consensus target sits around EUR 16.50 to EUR 17.40, roughly where our own sum-of-the-parts lands. The disagreement is with the marginal price-setter, who marked this stock back to its 52-week low within two sessions of a first-half beat and a reaffirmed guide.

The assumption embedded in the tape is terminal decline. At EUR 12.77 the enterprise is being valued at about 7 times operating profit and the equity at under 9 times earnings with a free-cash-flow yield near 16%. That is the arithmetic of a business the market expects to earn less every year. The record says otherwise: five consecutive years of higher net profit (EUR 126m, 168m, 163m, 170m, 185m), EBITDA above EUR 1 billion for the first time since 2019, free cash flow up 21% in 2025, fuel-tank share up from 21% to 23% against a 30% target for 2030, and revenue that grew 0.4% like-for-like in the first half of 2026 against a market that fell 1.0%. The specific street assumption we would contest is that European exposure - about half of revenue - is a permanent value sink. Half the revenue is European; the order book is not. Two-thirds of 2025 order intake was outside Europe, and the growth in the first half of 2026 came from North America, Korea, Japan and India.

Where we agree with the market, and this is why the disagreement does not translate into an immediate purchase: the return on capital. Six percent on capital employed, 1.8% net margin, and effectively no tangible book value once goodwill and intangibles are stripped out. The equity's value here comes from repaying debt, not from compounding - a slower and less certain path than a re-rating, and one that a single bad acquisition can suspend. The market is not wrong to price a low-return business at a low multiple. It is wrong to price it as though the profits were going away.

It is the one event in the file capable of moving the shares materially in the next quarter, and it is undated.

The second is the third-quarter revenue update, expected in late October 2026 on the company's usual quarterly cadence. That is the first evidence of whether resin and energy costs are being recovered through pricing, which is the question management refused to answer on 22 July, and the first read on whether the second-half cash bridge is holding.

The third, and the real test of the thesis, is the full-year results in late February 2027. That is where the three-part promise gets settled: free cash flow above EUR 297m, operating profit and net profit above 2025, and net debt below EUR 1,409m. The debt leg is already comfortably ahead at EUR 1,320m as of 30 June. A clean delivery would be the fourth consecutive year of meeting a publicly stated target and would make the 9-times earnings multiple much harder for the market to defend.

What is not a forcing function, and should be discounted to zero: the European industrial local-content framework. Management confirmed on 22 July that there is no timeframe, that alignment between carmakers, suppliers and member states is incomplete, and that it may arrive 'a bit too late'. And there is no governance or activist path at all - with 74.56% of the votes held by the family holding company, no strategic review, break-up or premium bid can be forced from outside.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next three to nine months, and it has four distinct hazards.

First and most acute, resin and energy. OPmobility converts polymer, so its swing costs track oil, and oil has moved sharply the wrong way: Brent has risen roughly a quarter since early July on the reinstated blockade at the Strait of Hormuz. On 22 July management confirmed the first-half hit landed mainly in the second quarter, refused to size it, said resin prices are 'moving up again' after a brief window of relief, and warned that a prolonged conflict makes the cost base hard for the whole industry to sustain. Recovery runs through contractual indexation where it exists and negotiation where it does not, and it lags by a quarter or two. First-half operating profit was already 3.6% lower in euros than a year earlier on flat revenue; the second half starts from a worse cost base.

Second, the shape of second-half cash generation. The chief financial officer volunteered the awkward detail himself: the first half took close to EUR 100m of working-capital benefit, the second half will see lower factoring and a reversal of the supplier-payment initiative, so the free-cash-flow guidance must be met from operating cash generation while investment rises. First-half free cash flow was EUR 167m against a full-year target above EUR 297m. There is no cushion in that bridge.

Third, the acquisition. If the Hyundai Mobis lighting deal signs at a full price, net debt rises precisely when the market is paying for debt repayment. Management says it will not affect the deleveraging path; that is an objective, not a term sheet, and the price is undisclosed.

Fourth, two acknowledged but unprovisioned costs. Management said on 22 July that customer restructuring across European carmakers is accelerating and that a heavier wave would force more of their own, but 'today, it's not embedded in our figures'. And the trade architecture shifted on 24 July, two days after the results, when the Section 122 tariff lapsed by statute and the proposed Section 301 replacement - covering sixty economies, with Korea, Japan and India at the higher rate and not yet final - moved into its place. OPmobility's stated growth engines are North America and Asia, and the business it is negotiating to buy is Korean.

Compounding all of this is an information vacuum. The company publishes full accounts only twice a year. After the 22 July release the next scheduled disclosure is the third-quarter revenue update, on the company's usual quarterly cadence in late October, with full-year results not due until late February 2027. The stock has to absorb a deteriorating cost environment with no new data for roughly three months.
positioning_washout:
There is no yield-holder base left to force out, because that exit has already happened. The dividend was cut hard: EUR 95m was paid out in 2024 and only EUR 31m in 2025, before being set at EUR 0.49 per share for the 2025 year and paid on 30 April 2026 - a 37.7% payout ratio. Income funds that were going to leave over the cut left more than a year ago, and the current 3.8% yield is neither high enough to attract a dedicated income holder nor at risk of a further cut that would expel one.

The real positioning feature is the float, and it works against a re-rating rather than for one. Burelle SA held 60.63% of the shares and 74.56% of the votes at 31 December 2025, leaving roughly 38% of a EUR 1.83 billion company - about EUR 0.7 billion - in public hands. Two consequences follow. First, mechanically forced selling of the kind that creates a washout bottom is unlikely to arrive here: there is no index deletion pending, no covenant stress at 1.4 times leverage, and no controlling holder under pressure. Second, and more important, the thin float means the price responds disproportionately to ordinary institutional reallocation. The tape after the results shows exactly this - the shares rose about 4% to EUR 13.44 on 22 July on a first-half beat and a reaffirmed guide, then gave the entire move back within two sessions to close 24 July at EUR 12.73, within 1% of the 52-week low, on volumes under 70,000 shares. The screener's own positioning readings agree: a smart-money score of 10 out of 100 and neutral institutional flow. Nobody is being forced out, and nobody is being forced in. That is the profile of a stock that drifts until a fundamental event forces attention, which argues for buying it cheaply rather than promptly.

One further note: the controlling family has not been buying at the 52-week low, at least not visibly - the recorded insider buy ratio is zero. With a 60% holder that signal is weak, but its absence removes what would otherwise have been the single most persuasive confirmation available.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a real value case being offered at a price that is good but not yet good enough, in the wrong month.

What is genuinely attractive: OPmobility is doing what it says. Four targets set for 2025 were met, including a debt reduction that matched the promised euro figure to the million. Profit has risen five years running, EBITDA passed EUR 1 billion for the first time since 2019, and the first half of 2026 grew against a market that shrank. Net debt has fallen from EUR 1,577m to EUR 1,320m in eighteen months and leverage from 1.7 to 1.4 times, which is the best balance sheet in a peer group where Forvia lost more than its entire market value last year and Gestamp carries twice the leverage. At under 9 times earnings with a free-cash-flow yield near 16% and a 3.8% dividend, the shareholder is paid to wait while debt repayment quietly transfers 8-11% a year across from lenders. Our sum-of-the-parts says EUR 15.60, the screener's discounted-cash-flow model says EUR 16.10 and the analyst consensus says EUR 16.50 to EUR 17.40 - three independent routes to roughly the same 22-30% discount.

What holds us back is not the absence of a catalyst. The lighting acquisition is a soft, non-binding negotiation with no fixed date, and in this book that is neither a plus nor a penalty; we judge the residual value case on its own. Three other things hold us back.

First, the asymmetry is not there. The base case is EUR 15.60 and the adverse case is EUR 9.20 - roughly balanced, because debt is 42% of the enterprise value, so a 20% fall in enterprise value costs the shareholder about 35%. And there is no floor beneath it: tangible book value is effectively zero once EUR 2.1 billion of goodwill and intangibles are removed from EUR 2.1 billion of equity.

Second, the multiple discount to peers is smaller than it looks. Recomputed live today, OPmobility's enterprise trades at 7.3 times operating profit against a European peer median of 7.1 times. It is not cheap against its cohort at the enterprise level; the equity is cheap because it is levered, and because the whole cohort has de-rated together on one shared driver - European vehicle production. That is sector beta, not name-specific edge.

Third, and decisively for timing, the one live macro driver runs straight through this company's cost line. This is a polymer converter, resin and energy track oil, and oil has risen roughly a quarter since early July on the reinstated Hormuz blockade. Management confirmed the first-half hit was concentrated in the second quarter, declined to size it, and said the cost base gets harder the longer the conflict runs. The current market regime is explicit that oil-sensitive names should be de-risked mid-event and that positions should favour businesses whose outcome does not depend on the same unresolved factor as everything else in the book. OPmobility is the opposite of orthogonal to that factor. On top of it, the second-half cash bridge has to work without the roughly EUR 100m of working-capital help that carried the first half, and there is no scheduled disclosure until the late-October revenue update.

The tape agrees. The shares rose about 4% on the results and gave it all back within two sessions to close within 1% of the 52-week low. That is not a stock whose re-rating is under way.

So: wait for the wash-out, and name it. We would buy at EUR 11.00 or below, which turns a 22% discount into a 42% one and pushes the adverse case to within a few percent of the entry. We would also buy without that discount on either of two developments: the Hyundai Mobis lighting deal signed at a disclosed price that visibly leaves net debt on its downward path, or a third-quarter update in late October showing resin and energy costs being recovered in price. Absent one of those, this is a good business-quality-adjusted price on a mediocre business into a deteriorating cost quarter, and there is no reason to pay for it in July.

Judged purely as a value proposition - setting aside the catalyst and the regime entirely - it rates a notch higher than the timing call. A 22% discount, five years of delivered results, the best balance sheet in its peer group and a dividend while you wait is a buy-lean. The single ingredient that withholds full conviction is durability: a 6% return on capital and no tangible book value mean this franchise defends a position rather than compounds one.
