interrogator_dossier:
# OPmobility SE (OPM.PA) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 27 July 2026. Price used throughout: €12.77 on Euronext Paris (all figures in euros unless stated). Transcripts covered: the 2025 full-year results call of 25 February 2026 and the first-half 2026 results call of 22 July 2026.*

OPmobility is the company formerly known as Plastic Omnium. It makes the plastic parts on the outside of cars (bumpers, tailgates, body panels), headlamps and rear lamps, the pre-assembled "front-end modules" that OEMs bolt straight onto a line, and fuel and energy-storage systems (fuel tanks, battery packs, hydrogen tanks). It is controlled by the Burelle family holding company, which owned 60.63% of the shares and 74.56% of the votes at 31 December 2025.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

**The story has not changed between the two calls — which, for a supplier in this industry, is itself the finding.**

In February 2026, presenting for the first time as chief executive, Félicie Burelle framed 2025 around a single claim: "We took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did." The supporting story had four legs — regional diversification away from Europe, a fuel-tank business consolidating share while rivals exit, a lighting business recovering from a bad starting order book, and a balance sheet being paid down.

By July 2026 all four legs were still there, told in the same order, with the same vocabulary. What was added, not swapped in, was a competitiveness programme: "there is no growth without being more competitive in our market," with named workstreams in engineering efficiency, robotics and digitalisation described as multi-year. What was quietly dropped: nothing material. The hydrogen and "beyond automotive" ambition, which in earlier years carried a lot of the equity story at this company, has been demoted to a small, honest aside — in February the chief executive said beyond-automotive is a small share of sales, "pretty much focused on what is linked to the electrification, i.e., the battery packs and H2 activity." That demotion is a credibility gain, not a loss: the speculative leg was shrunk rather than inflated.

The genuinely new element across the two calls is the proposed purchase of Hyundai Mobis's lighting business — a memorandum of understanding signed 27 January 2026 covering a controlling stake in a unit with more than €1 billion of annual revenue. It was still unsigned at the July call.

The market backdrop got worse between the calls and management said so plainly. In February they had planned for a roughly flat 2026; in July they opened with "the forecast for the 2026 year is minus 2.3%," Chinese domestic sales down 20% in the half, Europe still below pre-COVID volumes, and the Middle East conflict feeding through to energy and resin costs.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Where it was said | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did" | Feb 2026 | Operating profit €440m → €490m (+11.4%); EBITDA €929m → €1,001m; net profit €170m → €185m (+9%); free cash flow €246m → €297m (+21%) | Holds on all four |
| "The debt was reduced in '25 by EUR 167 million and amounted to EUR 1.4 billion" | Feb 2026 (CFO) | Net debt €1,577m → €1,409m, a fall of €168m | Holds, to the million |
| "Net debt-to-EBITDA decreased from 1.7x to 1.4x" | Feb 2026 | Consistent with the two figures above | Holds |
| "First time since 2019 that the group is able to exceed EUR 1 billion in EBITDA" | Feb 2026 (CFO) | EBITDA €1,001m | Holds |
| Slight growth in a shrinking market | Jul 2026 | First-half revenue +0.4% like-for-like against a market down 1.0% | Holds |
| Operating margin "solid… 4.8% of our revenues" | Jul 2026 | €251m on €5,202m of consolidated revenue = 4.83%, the same percentage as a year earlier — but 3.6% lower in euros than the €260m of the prior first half | Holds as a percentage; the euro figure went backwards |
| Guidance for 2026 unchanged: operating profit, net profit and free cash flow all above 2025, net debt lower | Feb and Jul 2026 | First-half net profit €102m versus €90m (+13%); free cash flow €167m; net debt €1.32bn at 30 June, down €141m year on year and €90m since December | On track at the half |
| Fuel-tank share "increased from 21% to 23%… on track with the target we have of 30% by 2030" | Feb 2026 | Powertrain revenue +1.4% like-for-like in 2025 and about +5% in the first half of 2026, in a shrinking market — consistent with share gain | Consistent, though share itself is a company-supplied figure we cannot independently audit |

**Where the story is richer than the trajectory justifies.** Five years of results tell a duller story than the presentation does. Revenue went from €7.23bn (2021) to €10.22bn (2025), but almost all of that came from the 2022 lighting acquisition, not from organic growth — the last two years read €10.31bn, €10.48bn, €10.22bn, which is flat. Net profit over the same five years went €126m, €168m, €163m, €170m, €185m: a real but modest climb, compounding at about 10% a year off a small base. Earnings per share went €0.87 → €1.30.

**The return on capital is the number the narrative never touches.** Return on equity is 8.1% and return on capital employed about 6%. That is a business earning roughly its cost of capital, no more. Neither call addressed it. Every improvement management cites is an improvement in a low-return business, not an escape from one.

**Two data warnings for the director, which are data artefacts rather than company issues.** First, the screener's trailing-twelve-month figures for this name are wrong and inflated: it reports trailing earnings per share of €2.49 and trailing free cash flow of €921m. OPmobility reports twice a year, and the data feed has summed four half-year periods — that is two full years, not one. The true trailing twelve months is earnings per share of about €1.37 (€0.66 in the second half of 2025 plus €0.71 in the first half of 2026) and free cash flow of about €300m on the company's own definition. The dividend confirms it: the €0.49 per share paid on 30 April 2026 was stated as a 37.7% payout ratio, which only works against earnings of €1.30, not €2.49. Second, the reported drop in gross margin from about 11% to 9.4% is a line-item reclassification in the data feed, not an operating event — research and development expense fell from €262m to €95m in the same year, which is a tagging change. On the company's own reported basis, margins went the other way: operating margin 4.2% → 4.8%, EBITDA margin 8.9% → 9.8%.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Stable, with the emphasis shifting from offence to defence.**

February 2026 was the more offensive of the two calls. The language was about positioning and expansion: "actively positioning our company on the future mobility hot topics," "strong acceleration," "2/3 of our order intake for 2025 is targeting regions outside Europe," "144 launches… flawless launches."

July 2026 opened with three paragraphs of adverse context before a single number: fierce competition led by China, Europe still below pre-COVID volumes, "a lot of heavy restructuring underway that we are carefully monitoring," low visibility on the North American trade rules, and the Middle East. The framing sentence was defensive: "we focus on what we know and what we can influence."

That is not a loss of nerve — the guidance was reaffirmed in the same breath — but the centre of gravity moved from growth to cost. The competitiveness programme, robotics and digitalisation are efficiency language. The most telling single line came in answer to Thomas Besson's question about whether customer restructuring would force more of their own: "today, it's not embedded in our figures." That is management naming an unquantified future cost while declining to size it.

Specificity of guidance improved rather than degraded. In February the chief financial officer gave a hard tax-rate number (35%, stable into 2026) and an explicit free-cash-flow bridge. In July he did it again, and volunteered the awkward part unprompted: the first half leaned on working capital, and the second half must be carried by operating cash generation instead.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: high.**

The 2025 targets were set and then met on every line management chose to be measured on — margin, net profit, cash flow and debt — and the debt figure matched the euro amount they had promised. The 2026 guidance was set in February, reaffirmed at the first quarter, and reaffirmed again in July with the first half tracking it. When the market forecast moved against them (flat expected, minus 2.3% delivered), they did not restate the guidance downward and they did not pretend the market had not moved.

There is no sandbagging pattern visible. The 2025 targets were met, not smashed; the language is "in line with the guidance," not "well ahead."

The screener records zero earnings beats in six quarters. That is close to meaningless for this company and should not be read as a delivery failure: OPmobility publishes full accounts twice a year and revenue updates in between, so a quarterly beat-rate is being scored against periods for which the company does not report earnings.

The one genuine credibility scar is older and management was asked about it directly. The 2022 purchase of Varroc's lighting business came with a weak order book that took three years to work through — in February the chief financial officer conceded "lighting continued to suffer from the poor order book of… prior to the acquisition," and the chief executive called 2025 "a low point in terms of sales" for that division. Asked by Ross MacDonald whether the Hyundai Mobis deal risked a repeat, the answer was assertion rather than evidence: "the situation is totally — it's not comparable… a very sizable business with 1 leading OEM. More than 90% of its sales engaged with that." That is a promise about a business whose order book we cannot see, made by a team that got the last one wrong.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three subjects recur, and management handles them very differently.

**Working capital and the shape of second-half cash flow.** Pushed by Ross MacDonald in February and again in July, and by Thomas Besson in July. The answers were direct and unflattering to the near term: the first half took close to €100m of working-capital benefit, the second half will see lower factoring and a reversal of the supplier-payment initiative, so gross cash generation has to do the work while capital spending rises. Analysts keep asking because this is where a miss would come from, and management is not hiding it.

**Raw materials and price recovery.** José Asumendi asked in July for the size of the raw-material hit and whether prices could be recovered in the second half. He did not get a number: "we won't comment too much on the amount… the impact was mainly on Q2." That is the clearest non-answer in either call, and it sits on the most live risk in the business. Management did concede the direction: resin prices had a brief window of relief and are "moving up again," recovery runs through contractual clauses where they exist and negotiation where they do not, and "the more the conflict last… the more it will be difficult for the whole industry to sustain over the long run."

**The Hyundai Mobis price and its balance-sheet effect.** Asked in February and twice in July. Management will say only that the figures disclosed exclude the project entirely and that they are "taking the objective of that acquisition not to impact our deleveraging strategy." An objective is not a term sheet. On timing, the July answer was "we are still in the summer" — a signal, not a date.

The topic analysts are *not* pressing, and should be, is the return on capital. Nobody in either transcript asked why a business turning over €10bn of revenue converts it into €185m of profit, or what the competitiveness programme is worth in return-on-capital terms rather than margin points.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flag — the raw-material exposure is unquantified and getting worse (July 2026).** OPmobility converts polymer. Resin and energy are its swing costs, the first-half hit landed in the second quarter, management declined to size it, and the driver — the conflict affecting oil and energy — was still open at the time of the call and has since intensified. First-half operating profit was 3.6% lower in euros than a year earlier, and this is the most likely reason.

**Red flag — the second half has to generate cash a harder way (July 2026).** By the chief financial officer's own bridge, the first-half cash flow leaned on working capital and factoring that reverse in the second half, against rising investment.

**Red flag — a large acquisition is being negotiated in the dark by a team whose last lighting acquisition disappointed (January to July 2026).** The target is more than €1bn of revenue against a company with a €1.8bn market capitalisation; the price is undisclosed; the reassurance is verbal.

**Red flag — customer restructuring is acknowledged and explicitly not provisioned (July 2026).** "Today, it's not embedded in our figures."

**Red flag — the lighting recovery has been promised for three years running.** In February management said lighting "should be back on a growth track in subsequent years." That sentence, in some form, has now been said about this division for three consecutive years. The first half of 2026 finally showed it turning, with seven launches, so the flag is close to clearing — but it is not yet cleared.

**Green flag — four consecutive targets met and a debt number that matched to the million (February 2026).** This is the strongest single item in the file.

**Green flag — deleveraging is real and continuing (February and July 2026).** Net debt €1,577m → €1,409m → €1,320m at 30 June 2026, leverage 1.7x → 1.4x. On an enterprise value of roughly €3.2bn against an equity value of €1.8bn, every euro of debt repaid moves to the shareholder.

**Green flag — the company is outgrowing a shrinking market, in the right places (July 2026).** North America and Asia excluding China led first-half growth; the Chinese joint venture tracked its market; two-thirds of 2025 order intake was outside Europe. Growth is coming from where the volume is, not from where the legacy is.

**Green flag — the speculative leg was shrunk rather than inflated.** Hydrogen and "beyond automotive" are presented as small and adjacent, with the robotaxi programme described honestly: "the start has been a bit lower than expected in terms of volume and in terms of complexity as well." A management team that under-claims its most fashionable business is a management team worth listening to on its unfashionable ones.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The customer list is being rebuilt, and the names have changed.** In February the launches cited were Mercedes, Jeep and an unnamed American electric-vehicle maker. In July the awards cited were Chery, Kia, Ford, Maruti Suzuki, BYD and programmes in India and Korea. The Chinese and Korean names moved from the periphery to the centre of the slide in five months. Management is explicit about the intent — "confirming this pivoting in terms of customer portfolio that we are operating."

**"Local for local" has become a stated hedge rather than a footprint statistic.** In February the 150-plant footprint was described as proximity to customers. In July it was described as protection: "we are pretty much local for local. So that's a big help when it comes to mitigating the impact of those events." The same asset, reframed from commercial advantage to trade-war insulation.

**Two words have disappeared from the growth story: Europe and electrification.** Europe is now discussed as a place to "consolidate" while growth happens elsewhere, and management has stopped presenting the shift to electric vehicles as its own growth driver — in July, slower electrification was cited as a *tailwind* for the fuel-tank business. That is an honest reversal, and it is the tell that the company now sees itself as a powertrain-agnostic parts maker rather than an electrification story.

**Management is lobbying in public and expects little.** On the European local-content framework: "we should have a framework… the alignment is not full… it takes a bit of time, but we are pushing so that it happens quickly. Otherwise, it would be a bit too late." A chief executive saying a policy may arrive too late is telling you not to underwrite it.

**The dividend answer was a policy statement, not a number.** Asked in February whether the €0.49 dividend would be defended, the answer was "we always have a policy of serving dividend to the shareholders. So that should remain the case." Given the acquisition being negotiated, the absence of a commitment to the level is deliberate.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: stable.**

This is a competently run, family-controlled, low-return industrial business that is doing exactly what it says it will do, in a market that is shrinking around it. Profit has risen five years running, cash flow is real, the balance sheet is being repaired on schedule, and the company has grown ahead of its end market in each of the last two reporting periods. It is not strengthening in the sense of earning better returns on capital — return on capital employed is stuck near 6% — and it is not deteriorating either.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** The equity is a leveraged claim on a business whose value moves slowly. Net debt of €1.32bn sits against an equity value of about €1.8bn, so debt is roughly 42% of the enterprise. That cuts both ways and the director must decide which side matters more over the holding period. Repaying €150m–200m of debt a year transfers roughly 8–11% a year to the equity at an unchanged enterprise value — that is the quiet engine of the thesis. But the same leverage means a 20% fall in enterprise value costs the shareholder about 35%. And the near-term cost driver — resin and energy — is not under management's control, was explicitly left unsized in July, and is deteriorating.

**Economic moat: narrow, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is scale-cost with a program-level switching cost: OPmobility is the world's largest maker of exterior body parts and holds about 23% of the fuel-tank market, its plants sit next to customer assembly lines, and once a part is tooled into a vehicle platform it stays there for the five-to-seven-year life of the programme. That is a real barrier, and it explains why the company has taken share while smaller rivals exited. But the evidence says the barrier does not convert into excess returns: return on capital employed of about 6% and net margin of 1.8% mean the customers, not the supplier, keep the surplus. The moat is genuine and it is not eroding — operating margin rose from 4.2% to 4.8% and EBITDA margin from 8.9% to 9.8% over 2024–2025, and the fuel-tank share is going up, not down — but a narrow moat at 6% returns is a defence of a modest position, not a compounding machine.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The structural risk is the long-run displacement of internal-combustion components by electrification, which over a fifteen-to-twenty year horizon takes the fuel-tank profit pool toward zero. That matters because Powertrain is the highest-margin segment (5.5% versus 2.7% for modules). But three things keep it short of terminal. It is only about 23% of revenue. The runway is long and currently lengthening — hybrids need tanks, and management named slower electrification as a first-half tailwind. And roughly three-quarters of the group — bumpers, body panels, lamps and front-end modules — is indifferent to what powers the car. The cheapness here is therefore best read as a fear print on a cyclical, leveraged, low-return business, not as a structurally shrinking base. It is not a value trap; it is a low-quality asset at a low price, which is a different and more ordinary proposition.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that the market is charging a distressed price for a business that is not distressed. OPmobility - the French supplier formerly called Plastic Omnium - makes the plastic parts on the outside of cars, headlamps, pre-assembled front-end modules and fuel and energy-storage systems. At EUR 12.77 on Euronext Paris the entire equity costs about EUR 1.83 billion. Against that sits roughly EUR 300 million a year of free cash flow on the company's own definition (EUR 297m in 2025, guided higher for 2026), which is a free-cash-flow yield near 16%, and about EUR 1.40 of likely 2026 earnings per share, which is under 9 times. Those are the prices you pay for a business you expect to shrink.

The evidence says it is not shrinking. Net profit has risen five years running, from EUR 126m in 2021 to EUR 185m in 2025. EBITDA passed EUR 1 billion in 2025 for the first time since 2019. Free cash flow rose 21% to EUR 297m. In the first half of 2026, reported on 22 July, revenue grew 0.4% on a like-for-like basis (stripping out currency and acquisitions) while global vehicle production fell 1.0%, net profit rose 13% to EUR 102m, and the operating margin held at 4.8% of sales. Full-year guidance - higher operating profit, higher net profit, higher free cash flow, lower debt - was reaffirmed unchanged for the third time this year.

The engine of the thesis is deleveraging, not growth. Net debt has gone EUR 1,577m (end 2024) to EUR 1,409m (end 2025) to EUR 1,320m at 30 June 2026, and leverage from 1.7 times EBITDA to 1.4 times. Debt is about 42% of the enterprise value here, so with the enterprise value unchanged, repaying EUR 150-200m of debt a year moves 8-11% a year across to the shareholder. Add a 3.8% dividend (EUR 0.49 per share, paid 30 April 2026) and the shareholder is being paid to wait while the balance sheet does the work.

The operating case has three specific supports. First, the fuel-tank business is consolidating a market that rivals are leaving: share went from 21% to 23% in 2025 against a 30% target for 2030, and management said in February 2026 that some competitors are 'decreasing, even disappearing'. It is also the highest-margin segment (5.5%) and it is currently being helped, not hurt, by slower electrification - a hybrid still needs a tank. Second, the lighting business, which has been the drag since the 2022 Varroc purchase came with a weak order book, finally inflected: seven launches in the first half of 2026 with more to come, and management calls 2025 'a low point in terms of sales' for that unit. Third, the customer base is being rebuilt where the volume actually is - two-thirds of 2025 order intake was outside Europe, and the awards named in July were Chery, Kia, Ford, Maruti Suzuki and Indian and Korean programmes rather than the European incumbents.

There is unpriced optionality in the proposed purchase of Hyundai Mobis's lighting business, a unit with more than EUR 1 billion of annual revenue, on which OPmobility signed a memorandum of understanding on 27 January 2026 and was named preferred bidder. If it lands at a sensible price it doubles the scale of the weakest division and hands OPmobility a direct commercial route into Hyundai and Kia, the fastest-growing volume group outside China.

What has to hold for this to work: resin and energy costs need to be recovered through contract indexation and negotiation within two to three quarters rather than permanently absorbed; the second half of 2026 has to generate cash from operations rather than from the working-capital and factoring pull that carried the first half; the Hyundai Mobis deal has to be signed at a price that does not interrupt debt repayment; and European vehicle production has to stop getting worse, not necessarily get better.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that this is an ordinary, low-return, leveraged cyclical whose cheapness is not a mispricing but a fair price, and that the next two or three quarters are the wrong ones to own it.

Start with quality. OPmobility converts EUR 10.2 billion of revenue into EUR 185 million of net profit - a 1.8% net margin - and earns about 6% on capital employed and 8.1% on equity. That is a business earning roughly its cost of capital and no more. Neither of the two earnings calls in the file addresses this, and no analyst asked. Tangible book value is effectively zero: shareholders' equity of EUR 2,119m at end-2025 is entirely accounted for by EUR 1,292m of goodwill and EUR 799m of other intangibles. There is no asset floor beneath the equity, only the cash flow.

Then the leverage. Net debt of EUR 1.32 billion sits against an equity value of about EUR 1.83 billion. That is the reason the equity screens cheap on earnings and free cash flow while the enterprise is priced roughly in line with its peers. The arithmetic is symmetrical and unforgiving: a 20% fall in enterprise value costs the shareholder about 35%.

The live risk is raw materials, and it is deteriorating. This is a polymer converter; resin and energy are its swing costs and they track oil. On the 22 July call management confirmed the first-half hit landed mainly in the second quarter, refused to size it - 'we won't comment too much on the amount' - said resin had a brief window of relief and is 'moving up again', and warned that 'the more the conflict last and it impacts the cost of energy and resin, the more it will be difficult for the whole industry to sustain over the long run'. Brent crude has risen roughly a quarter since early July on the reinstated Hormuz blockade. First-half operating profit was already 3.6% lower in euros than a year earlier despite flat revenue; the second half faces a worse cost base with no contracted recovery mechanism disclosed.

The cash-flow shape for the second half is the most likely place for a guidance miss, and the chief financial officer said so himself: the first half took close to EUR 100m of working-capital benefit, the second half will see lower factoring and the reversal of a supplier-payment initiative, so the free-cash-flow target has to be met out of operating cash generation while investment rises. Free cash flow of EUR 167m in the first half against a full-year target above EUR 297m leaves no room for the working capital to bite harder than planned.

The acquisition is a real balance-sheet risk, not just optionality. OPmobility is negotiating for a business with over EUR 1 billion of revenue while its own market capitalisation is EUR 1.8 billion, the price is undisclosed, and the only reassurance is verbal - 'we are taking the objective of that acquisition not to impact our deleveraging strategy'. That is an intention, not a term sheet. The precedent is unhelpful: the 2022 Varroc lighting purchase arrived with an order book so weak it took three years to work off, and management's answer to that comparison in February 2026 was assertion rather than evidence.

Two further costs are acknowledged and unquantified. Customer restructuring across European carmakers is accelerating, and management said in July that a heavier wave would force more of their own, but 'today, it's not embedded in our figures'. And the European local-content framework the company is lobbying for is undated, with the chief executive herself warning it might arrive 'a bit too late'.

Finally, there is no structural path to a forced re-rating. Burelle SA held 60.63% of the shares and 74.56% of the votes at 31 December 2025. There is no activist route, no takeover route and no break-up route. The float is roughly 38% of a EUR 1.8 billion company - about EUR 0.7 billion - which is thin enough that the stock can drift regardless of the fundamentals. That is visible in the tape: the shares rose about 4% to EUR 13.44 on the 22 July results and gave the whole move back within two sessions, closing 24 July at EUR 12.73, within 1% of the 52-week low.

What would confirm the bear: a third-quarter revenue update in late October showing no margin recovery on resin, or an acquisition announced at a price that lifts net debt back above EUR 1.5 billion.

Where we disagree with the market is not with the published analyst targets - five of six covering analysts rate the shares a buy and the consensus target sits around EUR 16.50 to EUR 17.40, roughly where our own sum-of-the-parts lands. The disagreement is with the marginal price-setter, who marked this stock back to its 52-week low within two sessions of a first-half beat and a reaffirmed guide.

The assumption embedded in the tape is terminal decline. At EUR 12.77 the enterprise is being valued at about 7 times operating profit and the equity at under 9 times earnings with a free-cash-flow yield near 16%. That is the arithmetic of a business the market expects to earn less every year. The record says otherwise: five consecutive years of higher net profit (EUR 126m, 168m, 163m, 170m, 185m), EBITDA above EUR 1 billion for the first time since 2019, free cash flow up 21% in 2025, fuel-tank share up from 21% to 23% against a 30% target for 2030, and revenue that grew 0.4% like-for-like in the first half of 2026 against a market that fell 1.0%. The specific street assumption we would contest is that European exposure - about half of revenue - is a permanent value sink. Half the revenue is European; the order book is not. Two-thirds of 2025 order intake was outside Europe, and the growth in the first half of 2026 came from North America, Korea, Japan and India.

Where we agree with the market, and this is why the disagreement does not translate into an immediate purchase: the return on capital. Six percent on capital employed, 1.8% net margin, and effectively no tangible book value once goodwill and intangibles are stripped out. The equity's value here comes from repaying debt, not from compounding - a slower and less certain path than a re-rating, and one that a single bad acquisition can suspend. The market is not wrong to price a low-return business at a low multiple. It is wrong to price it as though the profits were going away.
forcing_function:
There are three candidates and none of them is a hard, dated event, which is the honest summary of this setup.

The nearest is the signature of the Hyundai Mobis lighting transaction. The memorandum of understanding of 27 January 2026 states an intent to reach a final agreement during 2026, and on 22 July management pointed at the immediate window with 'we are still in the summer'. This forces a re-rating in either direction: a disclosed price that leaves the debt-repayment path intact removes the single largest unknown hanging over the equity, and a full price paid with the balance sheet confirms the bear. It is the one event in the file capable of moving the shares materially in the next quarter, and it is undated.

The second is the third-quarter revenue update, expected in late October 2026 on the company's usual quarterly cadence. That is the first evidence of whether resin and energy costs are being recovered through pricing, which is the question management refused to answer on 22 July, and the first read on whether the second-half cash bridge is holding.

The third, and the real test of the thesis, is the full-year results in late February 2027. That is where the three-part promise gets settled: free cash flow above EUR 297m, operating profit and net profit above 2025, and net debt below EUR 1,409m. The debt leg is already comfortably ahead at EUR 1,320m as of 30 June. A clean delivery would be the fourth consecutive year of meeting a publicly stated target and would make the 9-times earnings multiple much harder for the market to defend.

What is not a forcing function, and should be discounted to zero: the European industrial local-content framework. Management confirmed on 22 July that there is no timeframe, that alignment between carmakers, suppliers and member states is incomplete, and that it may arrive 'a bit too late'. And there is no governance or activist path at all - with 74.56% of the votes held by the family holding company, no strategic review, break-up or premium bid can be forced from outside.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next three to nine months, and it has four distinct hazards.

First and most acute, resin and energy. OPmobility converts polymer, so its swing costs track oil, and oil has moved sharply the wrong way: Brent has risen roughly a quarter since early July on the reinstated blockade at the Strait of Hormuz. On 22 July management confirmed the first-half hit landed mainly in the second quarter, refused to size it, said resin prices are 'moving up again' after a brief window of relief, and warned that a prolonged conflict makes the cost base hard for the whole industry to sustain. Recovery runs through contractual indexation where it exists and negotiation where it does not, and it lags by a quarter or two. First-half operating profit was already 3.6% lower in euros than a year earlier on flat revenue; the second half starts from a worse cost base.

Second, the shape of second-half cash generation. The chief financial officer volunteered the awkward detail himself: the first half took close to EUR 100m of working-capital benefit, the second half will see lower factoring and a reversal of the supplier-payment initiative, so the free-cash-flow guidance must be met from operating cash generation while investment rises. First-half free cash flow was EUR 167m against a full-year target above EUR 297m. There is no cushion in that bridge.

Third, the acquisition. If the Hyundai Mobis lighting deal signs at a full price, net debt rises precisely when the market is paying for debt repayment. Management says it will not affect the deleveraging path; that is an objective, not a term sheet, and the price is undisclosed.

Fourth, two acknowledged but unprovisioned costs. Management said on 22 July that customer restructuring across European carmakers is accelerating and that a heavier wave would force more of their own, but 'today, it's not embedded in our figures'. And the trade architecture shifted on 24 July, two days after the results, when the Section 122 tariff lapsed by statute and the proposed Section 301 replacement - covering sixty economies, with Korea, Japan and India at the higher rate and not yet final - moved into its place. OPmobility's stated growth engines are North America and Asia, and the business it is negotiating to buy is Korean.

Compounding all of this is an information vacuum. The company publishes full accounts only twice a year. After the 22 July release the next scheduled disclosure is the third-quarter revenue update, on the company's usual quarterly cadence in late October, with full-year results not due until late February 2027. The stock has to absorb a deteriorating cost environment with no new data for roughly three months.
positioning_washout:
There is no yield-holder base left to force out, because that exit has already happened. The dividend was cut hard: EUR 95m was paid out in 2024 and only EUR 31m in 2025, before being set at EUR 0.49 per share for the 2025 year and paid on 30 April 2026 - a 37.7% payout ratio. Income funds that were going to leave over the cut left more than a year ago, and the current 3.8% yield is neither high enough to attract a dedicated income holder nor at risk of a further cut that would expel one.

The real positioning feature is the float, and it works against a re-rating rather than for one. Burelle SA held 60.63% of the shares and 74.56% of the votes at 31 December 2025, leaving roughly 38% of a EUR 1.83 billion company - about EUR 0.7 billion - in public hands. Two consequences follow. First, mechanically forced selling of the kind that creates a washout bottom is unlikely to arrive here: there is no index deletion pending, no covenant stress at 1.4 times leverage, and no controlling holder under pressure. Second, and more important, the thin float means the price responds disproportionately to ordinary institutional reallocation. The tape after the results shows exactly this - the shares rose about 4% to EUR 13.44 on 22 July on a first-half beat and a reaffirmed guide, then gave the entire move back within two sessions to close 24 July at EUR 12.73, within 1% of the 52-week low, on volumes under 70,000 shares. The screener's own positioning readings agree: a smart-money score of 10 out of 100 and neutral institutional flow. Nobody is being forced out, and nobody is being forced in. That is the profile of a stock that drifts until a fundamental event forces attention, which argues for buying it cheaply rather than promptly.

One further note: the controlling family has not been buying at the 52-week low, at least not visibly - the recorded insider buy ratio is zero. With a 60% holder that signal is weak, but its absence removes what would otherwise have been the single most persuasive confirmation available.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a real value case being offered at a price that is good but not yet good enough, in the wrong month.

What is genuinely attractive: OPmobility is doing what it says. Four targets set for 2025 were met, including a debt reduction that matched the promised euro figure to the million. Profit has risen five years running, EBITDA passed EUR 1 billion for the first time since 2019, and the first half of 2026 grew against a market that shrank. Net debt has fallen from EUR 1,577m to EUR 1,320m in eighteen months and leverage from 1.7 to 1.4 times, which is the best balance sheet in a peer group where Forvia lost more than its entire market value last year and Gestamp carries twice the leverage. At under 9 times earnings with a free-cash-flow yield near 16% and a 3.8% dividend, the shareholder is paid to wait while debt repayment quietly transfers 8-11% a year across from lenders. Our sum-of-the-parts says EUR 15.60, the screener's discounted-cash-flow model says EUR 16.10 and the analyst consensus says EUR 16.50 to EUR 17.40 - three independent routes to roughly the same 22-30% discount.

What holds us back is not the absence of a catalyst. The lighting acquisition is a soft, non-binding negotiation with no fixed date, and in this book that is neither a plus nor a penalty; we judge the residual value case on its own. Three other things hold us back.

First, the asymmetry is not there. The base case is EUR 15.60 and the adverse case is EUR 9.20 - roughly balanced, because debt is 42% of the enterprise value, so a 20% fall in enterprise value costs the shareholder about 35%. And there is no floor beneath it: tangible book value is effectively zero once EUR 2.1 billion of goodwill and intangibles are removed from EUR 2.1 billion of equity.

Second, the multiple discount to peers is smaller than it looks. Recomputed live today, OPmobility's enterprise trades at 7.3 times operating profit against a European peer median of 7.1 times. It is not cheap against its cohort at the enterprise level; the equity is cheap because it is levered, and because the whole cohort has de-rated together on one shared driver - European vehicle production. That is sector beta, not name-specific edge.

Third, and decisively for timing, the one live macro driver runs straight through this company's cost line. This is a polymer converter, resin and energy track oil, and oil has risen roughly a quarter since early July on the reinstated Hormuz blockade. Management confirmed the first-half hit was concentrated in the second quarter, declined to size it, and said the cost base gets harder the longer the conflict runs. The current market regime is explicit that oil-sensitive names should be de-risked mid-event and that positions should favour businesses whose outcome does not depend on the same unresolved factor as everything else in the book. OPmobility is the opposite of orthogonal to that factor. On top of it, the second-half cash bridge has to work without the roughly EUR 100m of working-capital help that carried the first half, and there is no scheduled disclosure until the late-October revenue update.

The tape agrees. The shares rose about 4% on the results and gave it all back within two sessions to close within 1% of the 52-week low. That is not a stock whose re-rating is under way.

So: wait for the wash-out, and name it. We would buy at EUR 11.00 or below, which turns a 22% discount into a 42% one and pushes the adverse case to within a few percent of the entry. We would also buy without that discount on either of two developments: the Hyundai Mobis lighting deal signed at a disclosed price that visibly leaves net debt on its downward path, or a third-quarter update in late October showing resin and energy costs being recovered in price. Absent one of those, this is a good business-quality-adjusted price on a mediocre business into a deteriorating cost quarter, and there is no reason to pay for it in July.

Judged purely as a value proposition - setting aside the catalyst and the regime entirely - it rates a notch higher than the timing call. A 22% discount, five years of delivered results, the best balance sheet in its peer group and a dividend while you wait is a buy-lean. The single ingredient that withholds full conviction is durability: a 6% return on capital and no tangible book value mean this franchise defends a position rather than compounds one.

# OPmobility SE (OPM.PA) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 27 July 2026. Price used throughout: €12.77 on Euronext Paris (all figures in euros unless stated). Transcripts covered: the 2025 full-year results call of 25 February 2026 and the first-half 2026 results call of 22 July 2026.*

OPmobility is the company formerly known as Plastic Omnium. It makes the plastic parts on the outside of cars (bumpers, tailgates, body panels), headlamps and rear lamps, the pre-assembled "front-end modules" that OEMs bolt straight onto a line, and fuel and energy-storage systems (fuel tanks, battery packs, hydrogen tanks). It is controlled by the Burelle family holding company, which owned 60.63% of the shares and 74.56% of the votes at 31 December 2025.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

**The story has not changed between the two calls — which, for a supplier in this industry, is itself the finding.**

In February 2026, presenting for the first time as chief executive, Félicie Burelle framed 2025 around a single claim: "We took the commitment to improve all of our KPIs, and we did." The supporting story had four legs — regional diversification away from Europe, a fuel-tank business consolidating share while rivals exit, a lighting business recovering from a bad starting order book, and a balance sheet being paid down.

By July 2026 all four legs were still there, told in the same order, with the same vocabulary. What was added, not swapped in, was a competitiveness programme: "there is no growth without being more competitive in our market," with named workstreams in engineering efficiency, robotics and digitalisation described as multi-year. What was quietly dropped: nothing material. The hydrogen and "beyond automotive" ambition, which in earlier years carried a lot of the equity story at this company, has been demoted to a small, honest aside — in February the chief executive said beyond-automotive is a small share of sales, "pretty much focused on what is linked to the electrification, i.e., the battery packs and H2 activity." That demotion is a credibility gain, not a loss: the speculative leg was shrunk rather than inflated.

The genuinely new element across the two calls is the proposed purchase of Hyundai Mobis's lighting business — a memorandum of understanding signed 27 January 2026 covering a controlling stake in a unit with more than €1 billion of annual revenue. It was still unsigned at the July call.

The market backdrop got worse between the calls and management said so plainly. In February they had planned for a roughly flat 2026; in July they opened with "the forecast for the 2026 year is minus 2.3%," Chinese domestic sales down 20% in the half, Europe still below pre-COVID volumes, and the Middle East conflict feeding through to energy and resin costs.

---

**Where the story is richer than the trajectory justifies.** Five years of results tell a duller story than the presentation does. The true trailing twelve months is earnings per share of about €1.37 (€0.66 in the second half of 2025 plus €0.71 in the first half of 2026) and free cash flow of about €300m on the company's own definition. The dividend confirms it: the €0.49 per share paid on 30 April 2026 was stated as a 37.7% payout ratio, which only works against earnings of €1.30, not €2.49. Second, the reported drop in gross margin from about 11% to 9.4% is a line-item reclassification in the data feed, not an operating event — research and development expense fell from €262m to €95m in the same year, which is a tagging change. On the company's own reported basis, margins went the other way: operating margin 4.2% → 4.8%, EBITDA margin 8.9% → 9.8%.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Stable, with the emphasis shifting from offence to defence.**

February 2026 was the more offensive of the two calls. The language was about positioning and expansion: "actively positioning our company on the future mobility hot topics," "strong acceleration," "2/3 of our order intake for 2025 is targeting regions outside Europe," "144 launches… flawless launches."

July 2026 opened with three paragraphs of adverse context before a single number: fierce competition led by China, Europe still below pre-COVID volumes, "a lot of heavy restructuring underway that we are carefully monitoring," low visibility on the North American trade rules, and the Middle East. The framing sentence was defensive: "we focus on what we know and what we can influence."

That is not a loss of nerve — the guidance was reaffirmed in the same breath — but the centre of gravity moved from growth to cost. The competitiveness programme, robotics and digitalisation are efficiency language. The most telling single line came in answer to Thomas Besson's question about whether customer restructuring would force more of their own: "today, it's not embedded in our figures." That is management naming an unquantified future cost while declining to size it.

Specificity of guidance improved rather than degraded. In February the chief financial officer gave a hard tax-rate number (35%, stable into 2026) and an explicit free-cash-flow bridge. In July he did it again, and volunteered the awkward part unprompted: the first half leaned on working capital, and the second half must be carried by operating cash generation instead.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: high.**

The 2025 targets were set and then met on every line management chose to be measured on — margin, net profit, cash flow and debt — and the debt figure matched the euro amount they had promised. The 2026 guidance was set in February, reaffirmed at the first quarter, and reaffirmed again in July with the first half tracking it. When the market forecast moved against them (flat expected, minus 2.3% delivered), they did not restate the guidance downward and they did not pretend the market had not moved.

There is no sandbagging pattern visible. The 2025 targets were met, not smashed; the language is "in line with the guidance," not "well ahead."

The screener records zero earnings beats in six quarters. That is close to meaningless for this company and should not be read as a delivery failure: OPmobility publishes full accounts twice a year and revenue updates in between, so a quarterly beat-rate is being scored against periods for which the company does not report earnings.

The one genuine credibility scar is older and management was asked about it directly. The 2022 purchase of Varroc's lighting business came with a weak order book that took three years to work through — in February the chief financial officer conceded "lighting continued to suffer from the poor order book of… prior to the acquisition," and the chief executive called 2025 "a low point in terms of sales" for that division. Asked by Ross MacDonald whether the Hyundai Mobis deal risked a repeat, the answer was assertion rather than evidence: "the situation is totally — it's not comparable… a very sizable business with 1 leading OEM. More than 90% of its sales engaged with that." That is a promise about a business whose order book we cannot see, made by a team that got the last one wrong.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three subjects recur, and management handles them very differently.

**Working capital and the shape of second-half cash flow.** Pushed by Ross MacDonald in February and again in July, and by Thomas Besson in July. The answers were direct and unflattering to the near term: the first half took close to €100m of working-capital benefit, the second half will see lower factoring and a reversal of the supplier-payment initiative, so gross cash generation has to do the work while capital spending rises. Analysts keep asking because this is where a miss would come from, and management is not hiding it.

**Raw materials and price recovery.** José Asumendi asked in July for the size of the raw-material hit and whether prices could be recovered in the second half. He did not get a number: "we won't comment too much on the amount… the impact was mainly on Q2." That is the clearest non-answer in either call, and it sits on the most live risk in the business. Management did concede the direction: resin prices had a brief window of relief and are "moving up again," recovery runs through contractual clauses where they exist and negotiation where they do not, and "the more the conflict last… the more it will be difficult for the whole industry to sustain over the long run."

**The Hyundai Mobis price and its balance-sheet effect.** Asked in February and twice in July. Management will say only that the figures disclosed exclude the project entirely and that they are "taking the objective of that acquisition not to impact our deleveraging strategy." An objective is not a term sheet. On timing, the July answer was "we are still in the summer" — a signal, not a date.

The topic analysts are *not* pressing, and should be, is the return on capital. Nobody in either transcript asked why a business turning over €10bn of revenue converts it into €185m of profit, or what the competitiveness programme is worth in return-on-capital terms rather than margin points.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flag — the raw-material exposure is unquantified and getting worse (July 2026).** OPmobility converts polymer. Resin and energy are its swing costs, the first-half hit landed in the second quarter, management declined to size it, and the driver — the conflict affecting oil and energy — was still open at the time of the call and has since intensified. First-half operating profit was 3.6% lower in euros than a year earlier, and this is the most likely reason.

**Red flag — the second half has to generate cash a harder way (July 2026).** By the chief financial officer's own bridge, the first-half cash flow leaned on working capital and factoring that reverse in the second half, against rising investment.

**Red flag — a large acquisition is being negotiated in the dark by a team whose last lighting acquisition disappointed (January to July 2026).** The target is more than €1bn of revenue against a company with a €1.8bn market capitalisation; the price is undisclosed; the reassurance is verbal.

**Red flag — customer restructuring is acknowledged and explicitly not provisioned (July 2026).** "Today, it's not embedded in our figures."

**Red flag — the lighting recovery has been promised for three years running.** In February management said lighting "should be back on a growth track in subsequent years." That sentence, in some form, has now been said about this division for three consecutive years. The first half of 2026 finally showed it turning, with seven launches, so the flag is close to clearing — but it is not yet cleared.

**Green flag — four consecutive targets met and a debt number that matched to the million (February 2026).** This is the strongest single item in the file.

**Green flag — deleveraging is real and continuing (February and July 2026).** Net debt €1,577m → €1,409m → €1,320m at 30 June 2026, leverage 1.7x → 1.4x. On an enterprise value of roughly €3.2bn against an equity value of €1.8bn, every euro of debt repaid moves to the shareholder.

**Green flag — the company is outgrowing a shrinking market, in the right places (July 2026).** North America and Asia excluding China led first-half growth; the Chinese joint venture tracked its market; two-thirds of 2025 order intake was outside Europe. Growth is coming from where the volume is, not from where the legacy is.

**Green flag — the speculative leg was shrunk rather than inflated.** Hydrogen and "beyond automotive" are presented as small and adjacent, with the robotaxi programme described honestly: "the start has been a bit lower than expected in terms of volume and in terms of complexity as well." A management team that under-claims its most fashionable business is a management team worth listening to on its unfashionable ones.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The customer list is being rebuilt, and the names have changed.** In February the launches cited were Mercedes, Jeep and an unnamed American electric-vehicle maker. In July the awards cited were Chery, Kia, Ford, Maruti Suzuki, BYD and programmes in India and Korea. The Chinese and Korean names moved from the periphery to the centre of the slide in five months. Management is explicit about the intent — "confirming this pivoting in terms of customer portfolio that we are operating."

**"Local for local" has become a stated hedge rather than a footprint statistic.** In February the 150-plant footprint was described as proximity to customers. In July it was described as protection: "we are pretty much local for local. So that's a big help when it comes to mitigating the impact of those events." The same asset, reframed from commercial advantage to trade-war insulation.

**Two words have disappeared from the growth story: Europe and electrification.** Europe is now discussed as a place to "consolidate" while growth happens elsewhere, and management has stopped presenting the shift to electric vehicles as its own growth driver — in July, slower electrification was cited as a *tailwind* for the fuel-tank business. That is an honest reversal, and it is the tell that the company now sees itself as a powertrain-agnostic parts maker rather than an electrification story.

**Management is lobbying in public and expects little.** On the European local-content framework: "we should have a framework… the alignment is not full… it takes a bit of time, but we are pushing so that it happens quickly. Otherwise, it would be a bit too late." A chief executive saying a policy may arrive too late is telling you not to underwrite it.

**The dividend answer was a policy statement, not a number.** Asked in February whether the €0.49 dividend would be defended, the answer was "we always have a policy of serving dividend to the shareholders. So that should remain the case." Given the acquisition being negotiated, the absence of a commitment to the level is deliberate.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: stable.**

This is a competently run, family-controlled, low-return industrial business that is doing exactly what it says it will do, in a market that is shrinking around it. Profit has risen five years running, cash flow is real, the balance sheet is being repaired on schedule, and the company has grown ahead of its end market in each of the last two reporting periods. It is not strengthening in the sense of earning better returns on capital — return on capital employed is stuck near 6% — and it is not deteriorating either.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** The equity is a leveraged claim on a business whose value moves slowly. Net debt of €1.32bn sits against an equity value of about €1.8bn, so debt is roughly 42% of the enterprise. That cuts both ways and the director must decide which side matters more over the holding period. Repaying €150m–200m of debt a year transfers roughly 8–11% a year to the equity at an unchanged enterprise value — that is the quiet engine of the thesis. But the same leverage means a 20% fall in enterprise value costs the shareholder about 35%. And the near-term cost driver — resin and energy — is not under management's control, was explicitly left unsized in July, and is deteriorating.

**Economic moat: narrow, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is scale-cost with a program-level switching cost: OPmobility is the world's largest maker of exterior body parts and holds about 23% of the fuel-tank market, its plants sit next to customer assembly lines, and once a part is tooled into a vehicle platform it stays there for the five-to-seven-year life of the programme. That is a real barrier, and it explains why the company has taken share while smaller rivals exited. But the evidence says the barrier does not convert into excess returns: return on capital employed of about 6% and net margin of 1.8% mean the customers, not the supplier, keep the surplus. The moat is genuine and it is not eroding — operating margin rose from 4.2% to 4.8% and EBITDA margin from 8.9% to 9.8% over 2024–2025, and the fuel-tank share is going up, not down — but a narrow moat at 6% returns is a defence of a modest position, not a compounding machine.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The structural risk is the long-run displacement of internal-combustion components by electrification, which over a fifteen-to-twenty year horizon takes the fuel-tank profit pool toward zero. That matters because Powertrain is the highest-margin segment (5.5% versus 2.7% for modules). But three things keep it short of terminal. It is only about 23% of revenue. The runway is long and currently lengthening — hybrids need tanks, and management named slower electrification as a first-half tailwind. And roughly three-quarters of the group — bumpers, body panels, lamps and front-end modules — is indifferent to what powers the car. The cheapness here is therefore best read as a fear print on a cyclical, leveraged, low-return business, not as a structurally shrinking base. It is not a value trap; it is a low-quality asset at a low price, which is a different and more ordinary proposition.
